utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. Welcome back after the long break. It's good to see you all again, and I hope very much that we will proceed in the same constructive way as we did before the summer recess and in the past of this trial. Yes. Let's look forward to the last part of the Prosecution case, probable 98 bis submissions, a possible Defence case, and let's co-operate in the same way. And I would like to mention again, that we appreciate the assistance and the support by all the staff of the different sections of this Tribunal. Before the witness will be brought in, I would like to raise one matter. On the 4th of July this year, the OTP notified us regarding remaining witnesses. One part of this notification was related to six proposed 92 quater witnesses. In this chapter, in fact, there is a list of seven witnesses. I quote: "The Prosecution will file prior to the summer recess a Rule 92 quater motion regarding the following six," in fact seven, "witnesses, all of whom are suffering from bodily or mental condition rendering them unable to testify orally." We received one motion by the Prosecution regarding one witness, PW-006, but we didn't receive any other motion by the Prosecution. And therefore, I would like to ask you, Mr. McCloskey, if you can give us an update if you are intending to file any other motions, which should be quite urgent now as we are approaching the end of the Prosecution case, or if the Prosecution intends to withdraw these six remaining witnesses. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours. Hello. It's good to be back. General Tolimir, Mr. Gajic, everyone. I have talked with the team about a couple of those witnesses, and I will check with them and get a better answer for you at the break. If we could go into private session just briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the meantime, I would like to ask you, Mr. McCloskey, about the witnesses to be called in September. Usually, we receive such a list in the middle of the previous month. We didn't receive something like that in the middle of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps you can inquire what is the case. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Our list that we filed for July, I am told it's the same. It's the same list of people that are remaining and -- but we will file that over again, and I have gone over the -- I saw six remaining witnesses, and I noted that they are all scheduled and those schedules have been confirmed, and we had based that on Mr. Butler testifying about the same time for the Defence as he did for the Prosecution, which Mr. Gajic has just confirmed to me that they expected to take the same time that the Prosecution took. So the schedule for those remaining people, it seems to be fairly solid as these things are based on the time that the Prosecution took for Mr. Butler, and I will have those as a reminder for us and something we'll send to you as well so you can see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would appreciate that. Thank you very much. Good afternoon, Mr. Butler. Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I hope for you, as well as all the other participants in this trial, that you have had a good vacation with some relaxation and recovery. Welcome back again, and I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning of your testimony still applies for this remainder of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir is continuing his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May there be peace in this house for all those present, and may God's will be done in these proceedings and not mine. I extend my greetings to the Trial Chamber, to Mr. President, Judges Nyambe and Mindua. I extend my greetings to Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Butler, and all the representatives of the Registry. And I wish all of you a good day's work today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Butler, last time we completed a portion of the document concerning the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and its attempts to link up with the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica. You stated that you had seen the document, and this was a document by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina which was, in fact, an activation of attacks out of the protected areas, safe areas, against the Army of Republika Srpska and the Main Staff. Perhaps we should look at this document once more e-court, thank you. And I have several questions for you on this issue. Thank you. D53. We can see it in both versions. This is a document issued by the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, its General Staff, Main Staff, dated the 17th of June, 1995. In other words, it was issued 15 days before the commencement of combat activities in the safe area of Srebrenica. It is entitled "Preparations for offensive combat operations, order." Let me quote this again: "Based -- or pursuant to a verbal order issued by the commander of the General Staff of the BH Army, army general Rasim Delic, and on the occasion of the great success achieved by units of the BH Army in the wide area around Sarajevo and Gorazde, as well as on the basis of intelligence, et cetera, I hereby issue the following order: "1. Execute all preparations in the command of the 28th Land Army Division to execute offensive combat operations with a view to liberating the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, overextending the aggressor forces and inflicting losses on them, co-ordinating action with the BH Army forces carrying out operations in the broader Sarajevo area." This is my question for you: Does it follow from this order that also the forces present in Gorazde as well as those in Srebrenica and Zepa were activated under this order? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I don't know if you could make that conclusion specifically. As you can see at the bottom of the page, it is addressed to the 28th Division Srebrenica, the 285th Brigade in Zepa, and to the command of the 2nd Corps. There is not a specific designator or anything that would indicate that the message or this order went directly to the forces in Gorazde. It may very well be that the command of the 2nd Corps did, in fact, pass these orders on and make such plans, but it's not inherent in this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. You -- do you know that there was only packet communications systems present in Srebrenica and that it could only communicate with Tuzla? Could there have been a circular communication from Srebrenica via Tuzla to Gorazde, if you know? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am only aware of the communications as they existed with respect to Srebrenica and Zepa. I do not know the specifics of the communications network for the ABiH dealing with Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. You do see that in line 2, behind the comma, it is stated: "... on the occasion of the great success achieved by units of the BH Army in the general area around Sarajevo and Gorazde." Does this mean that these units were involved in active combat activities and that they were successful to a certain degree in the Gorazde area? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that time-frame certainly the ABiH 1st Corps in and around Sarajevo was very active, and by their definition, they thought they were being somewhat successful. Although, quite frankly, they didn't achieve their ultimate goals. There were military operations around Gorazde, as indicated by the VRS documents, which necessitated the Drina Corps having to send at least one composite unit to the Trnovo battle-front in order to hold a portion of the line. So that is generally what I'm aware of of this one. Again, defining success or not, I think, as it goes, ultimately the ABiH 1st Corps was not successful because they ultimately were not able to break through the VRS siege line around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. My question didn't have to do with the extent of their success, rather, whether from the demilitarised area of Gorazde there were combat activities being carried out, as is stated in this document. Would you deny what the document states? Because it does allow for that possibility. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I mean the document says what the document says. I am not aware of any of the specific details of ABiH military operations out of Gorazde at that time. I just don't know the specifics of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please answer my question. Were there combat activities taking place from each of the safe areas in Bosnia; namely, Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde? Were you aware of this and did you see any documents to that effect? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. During the course of this time there were military operations out of the demilitarised areas by the ABiH, certainly from Srebrenica. We've talked about at length operations out of Zepa at about the same time. This has been the focus of my -- my study is in Srebrenica and Zepa. Again, I assume that they were out of Gorazde, but I am just not aware of the details in the same manner that I am for Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Do you know that Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde were in the rear of the Army of Republika Srpska and that they were separated from the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina? In other words, do you know that Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde were enclaves deep within the territory of Republika Srpska and separate from the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, you're correct. They all were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us as a soldier, should the Army of Republika Srpska have tolerated the attacks out of the enclaves into its rear, the attacks being directed against its population and the army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Setting aside my own personal views, which aren't really relevant to that answer, the fact is that the VRS did have to garrison the perimeters of those safe areas. As noted in their own documents, they were desperately short of manpower and believed that those forces could be used more successfully in other areas of the battle-field. So having to garrison those around the perimeters around those safe areas was causing a problem for the Army of Republika Srpska. Along the same vein, they were being attacked by the ABiH and having to respond to those various attacks. So whether or not they were tolerated or should have been tolerated or could have been tolerated, from a military perspective, the maintenance of those forces outside of the safe areas had a significantly detrimental impact to at least the military forces of the Army of Republika Srpska in Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Can you tell us, did you arrive at a conclusion that the Muslim army attacked out of the enclaves the rear of the Army of Republika Srpska thanks to the fact that they could not have been persecuted after the sabotage actions were taken in an area protected by UNPROFOR? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure I understand your question, sir. Could I ask you to just repeat or it or rephrase it. I just -- I'm not sure what you are trying to get at.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Let me repeat the question. Could the Army of Republika Srpska have destroyed the Muslim armed formations in the enclaves or would it have been prevented from doing so by UNPROFOR? And I mean as a result of these combat activities that would take place in the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly as evidenced by the events of July 1995, the VRS could and did have the physical capability of doing just that when the United Nations Protection Forces did not defend the safe areas. Whether the VRS recognised that earlier and could have done so earlier is always going to a question of history. But militarily speaking, the VRS did have the ability to do that. When they recognised that they had the ability is the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Butler, did you come across documents where, for instance, observers of the United Nations, like Kingori and others, stated that there were no combat activities in Srebrenica up until the commencement of the operation directed toward the strongholds held by personnel involved in sabotage actions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has been a while since I've reviewed the actual UN reports for the Srebrenica enclave for the first part of 1995. Keeping that in mind, even if I assume your point is true, the reality is that starting in the early part of 1999 [sic], the ABiH did start to restrict the ability of the United Nations forces inside the enclave to actively patrol the entire enclave and to monitor those forces. For example, restricting movement of the UN so they could not go into the Bandera triangle area where the bulk of the 28th Division was. So the fact that the UN may have been reporting that there was no activity or very limited activity is a reflection of what they were seeing because their view was limited by the ABiH in many respects.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think Mr. Butler said "1999" and I think that was just a mistake. It's page 10, line 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's "1999" in the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It should be 1995, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. In view of the fact that in 1995, from the spring until the fall of the Srebrenica enclave, the Muslim army carried out sabotage actions and even restricted UNPROFOR movement within protected areas, would you agree these were indicators that even within the protected areas the ABH opted for offensive actions as this report seems to indicate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, to the degree that I've testified that the ABiH, the 28th Division, was not demilitarised and did continue to conduct offensive combat operations outside of the enclave in support of broader ABiH objectives to tie down as much of the VRS as possible. So I believe that I've been consistent in that position that the 28th Division did, in fact, conduct those offensive operations through the early spring of January almost all the way up until July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: It's not really a question, it's just for my benefit. I am never very clear when people are talking about spring and fall. This is both to the Defence, so for my benefit I would appreciate if you could be more precise like mention a month and that sort of thing. I would appreciate, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes ma'am. And in this respect, I would say you certainly start to see that uptick in offensive activities by early March of 1995 consistent with the beginning of the major ABiH operation in and around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank Judge Nyambe for shedding light on this issue and correcting my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, were UN forces, with the authority of the United Nations, able to stop offensive operations from protective areas and thus prevent a conflict between the forces within the protected areas and the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I would say to that is, referring back to the United Nations' own report dealing with Srebrenica, one of the underlying themes that runs through that report is that there seemed to be a difference of opinion between the various organs of the United Nations that were responsible for administering the safe areas and defining what exactly that mandate meant on the ground. For example, as General Tolimir indicated, there was one group of people who thought that that particular mission was to enforce the demilitarisation. There was another group of people who believed it was to be a peacekeeping force. Quite frankly, one of the lessons learned out of Srebrenica from the United Nations' perspective is that they went into this particular mission not having a clear vision of what they were trying to accomplish after moving into Srebrenica and the other safe areas in 1993. With that as the background, I don't know in that context whether or not the UN in particular, or specifically the Dutch Battalion, felt it was their job to stop those offensive operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us whose offensive operations, offensive operations originating from the enclaves or the offensive operations by the VRS aimed at the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that would be the ABiH military operations originating from inside the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Butler. Considering that you've just outlined the problems the UN faced within the enclaves, did you perhaps come across documents where the UN forces, the UNPROFOR, informed the United Nations that the Muslims wanted practically their protection from the VRS while continuing to mount their own operations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I can't right off of memory come to a specific document, but in doing this and doing this research, one of the themes that the UN believed was occurring was that the ABiH from inside the enclave was conducting military attacks and then seeking the shield of the United Nations forces in the enclaves in an effort to potentially forestall any retaliation by the Army of the Republika Srpska. The degree that has happened or did not happen is always going to be a matter of speculation, but it certainly was a generally widely-held opinion by the UN that that practice was going on, at least with respect to the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Before we move to the next document, I should like to ask you: Does this order practically activate operations from protected areas against the VRS on the part of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it specifically says and implements, this document, is that they want elements of the 28th Division, specifically the 285th Light Infantry Brigade in Zepa, to conduct offensive operations with a goal of preventing the protection regiment in Han Pijesak, which is the 65th Protection Regiment, from being able to disengage from that area of the battle-field and be available for use elsewhere. So that is what this document specifically says or directs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Perhaps I was not very clear in my question. If so, I'm sorry. But did the command of the BH Army deliberately involve the protected areas in the struggle against the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. By virtue of the orders that were to the military units with -- inside the safe areas, the command of the ABiH did, in fact, involve them. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this order refer to active operations from Gorazde and Sarajevo, where they are scoring successes, and does this speak of the commencement of an offensive and creating conditions for linking up the enclaves of Srebrenica and Gorazde with the BH Army and the territory held under its control?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I believe it is a very limited order. While it references many of those broader issues, I believe that the paragraph that best illustrates that is paragraph 2, where it discusses the planning of realistic tasks which will assure certain success on the basis of an accurate assessment in the potential of our forces in Srebrenica and Zepa. At the time the forces in Srebrenica and Zepa did not have those broad types of abilities. So in the context of what they could actually accomplish on the ground, this order lays out the broader framework of that but directs them to plan realistic combat operations which would have the goal of preventing the VRS from moving forces from the Srebrenica-Zepa area to Sarajevo and Gorazde. But I don't think that they anticipated that those realistic tasks would be to link both of the enclaves and liberate vast areas of territory then under control of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. My question was: Did the BH Army order demilitarised zones to mount active operations behind the lines of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As this document says, paragraph 2 is to plan realistic tasks. Paragraph 3 is that the General Staff will regulate by ordering the commencement of those tasks. So in that context, the General Staff of the army is ordering the forces in Srebrenica and Zepa to come up with realistic alternatives or realistic plans of what they can do and letting them know that at some future point that the ABiH would direct them to implement those tasks. That is what the order says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us as a soldier, did the author of the order realise that he would activate armed combat groups within the protected areas which would in turn cause the VRS to start pursuing these groups?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't ascribe to that type of a cause-and-effect situation, only in part because the way that you phrased that question it implies that before this, those particular combat forces were not active or that they had somehow been deactivated. The reality is that well before June of 1995, ABiH military forces did conduct combat operations and raids out of the enclave. 2nd Corps, their apparent headquarters were aware of those operations, and presumably the General Staff was aware of them as well. So I don't take it as a point in time in June of 1995 that the General Staff of the ABiH is flipping a switch with this order, so to speak, and activating those units. They were never deactivated for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Please tell us, did the UNPROFOR then know that the BH Army had combat units within demilitarised areas?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly the United Nations leadership in Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as the Dutch, recognised that within the Srebrenica enclave and the Zepa enclave, the ABiH military units did exist, were armed, and did participate in combat activities. As I discussed earlier, that wasn't a big secret, particularly given the fact that the Dutch in the Srebrenica enclave were prevented by the ABiH from observing certain parts of the enclave where those military forces were. So while the UN might not have had an accurate picture of the units and their combat capabilities, they obviously were aware that they existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. I apologise for not having shown you a document about this, because this is the second time you speak of this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D66 is the document I would like to see in e-court. It's a document from the 28th Division, dated 29 January 1995. Here we'll see it now on the screen in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You see the document was signed by the commander of that brigade, Naser Oric, in January of 1995. It says: "In view of the situation in Podgaj village, the situation that occurred on 9 January 1995, of which you have been informed in a timely manner, the command of the 8th Operations Group has restricted the movement of the UNPROFOR forces in the wider region of Suceska and Podgaj. "At about 1100 hours today, the commander of the Dutch battalion in Srebrenica ordered his patrols to enter the movement restriction area. In co-ordination with the commander of the 8th Operations Group, honouring the agreement reached with the UNPROFOR liaison officer after the warning was issued not to move in the aforementioned area, the commander of the 281st Eastern Bosnia Light Brigade blocked all UNPROFOR patrols and is still keeping them blocked. The Dutch battalion commander in this area was requested that ..." Et cetera, et cetera. Commander Naser Oric. Tell us, did you review such documentation? Why was the UNPROFOR banned from moving in the area of these villages, Suceska and Podgaj?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't review this document specifically, but again, as I have testified, I am generally aware that the UN was being restricted from various parts of the enclaves. I couldn't tell you in this particular document or these particular villages. I don't know why they would have been banned at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you seen any documents showing that the command of the UNPROFOR for Bosnia informed the UN Security Council that a certain number of their men were detained and their entry into the demilitarised zones was prohibited? And that was precisely what they were there for. It was their mandate to be in the demilitarised areas.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I recall I am generally aware of the incident you are talking about, but I don't know specifically that that issue was elevated to the UN Security Council. I am just not aware of that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As a soldier who has been in several theatres of war and served in other countries as well, would you say that an army under blockade and unable to perform its mission would inform its command, in this case the UN, about the problem, like Naser Oric informed his superiors?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that the Dutch at some juncture elevated this to their command in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Your specific question had to deal with the United Nations Security Council and whether they were informed. And my answer is, I don't know how far up the chain of the UN that that particular notification went. I mean, I just don't know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. But in the chain of command, does one need to inform one's superior and was the superior authority for the UNPROFOR commander the UN Security Council?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chain of command as it deals with forces that are part of the United Nations is a little less clear than that. And I guess maybe the best example to use would be what happened in July of 1995. As the various investigative commissions following Srebrenica at both the United Nations and the Dutch government noted, the Dutch Battalion, when their soldiers started to be placed under the custody of the VRS, on the 7th and 8th and 9th of July, those facts were being transmitted not only to the UN to be elevated to the UN people in Bosnia and beyond, but were also being transmitted to the Dutch national government through their Ministry of Defence. So clearly with respect to the Dutch military units in Srebrenica, they were keeping the United Nations informed, at least their superiors within the United Nations informed, as well as their own national governmental organs here in Holland. Again, going back to your question, did that elevate itself all the way up to the United Nations Security Council? I just don't know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This problem of 9 July, when the UNPROFOR issued the green order on operations against the VRS, will be discussed later when we come to another subject. Now, in this set of questions I would like to ask you: Did the UNPROFOR command in Sarajevo know that Muslims were making it impossible for the UNPROFOR in Srebrenica to carry out their mission? You say that Naser Oric is saying precisely this and he is inviting UNPROFOR commanders responsible for Bosnia and Herzegovina to come and solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, I am generally aware that the Dutch were reporting this issue up to Sarajevo, to the UN command there. I don't know a specific point in time where they would have gained awareness and I don't have a document that I can say that they knew on this particular date. But again going back to the United Nations report relative to Srebrenica, it does discuss the fact that the Dutch were reporting back to their superiors in Sarajevo that there were restrictions of movement as well as other issues that they were having with the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us as a soldier, did Rupert Smith as the UNPROFOR commander and his successors have the duty to report to their immediate superior, namely, the United Nations, that the UNPROFOR was disabled from carrying out its mandate? Were they supposed to do that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suspect that would be a better question for General Smith than it would for me. My knowledge of the UN and how it relates to Srebrenica is pretty limited to the actual issues related to the enclave. The broader issues of how the UN operated in Bosnia and the relationships General Smith had with other people with regard to that was just not a topic that I had to get into as part of my analysis, so I'm just not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just need to get back to the last question. Based on your experience as a military analyst, and I would like to believe expert, do you think the UN commanders, either in Srebrenica or in Sarajevo, had a duty to report to their superiors in the United Nations that the UNPROFOR was disabled from carrying out their mandate? I would like your answer to that question, if I may. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I expect that they would have a duty to report this up their chain of command. As I -- again, I recall from the United Nations report, it was known in Sarajevo. It was known in Zagreb [Realtime transcript read in error "Zvornik Brigade"], which was the headquarters for the entire UN operation dealing with the former Yugoslavia. What I don't know the answer to, and I expect it's readily available, is whether or not the entire story from the UN command in Zagreb was relayed in that manner to the United Nations Security Council in New York. I think when one goes and looks at that United Nations report about Srebrenica, it is very clear that there was a difference of opinion as to what should be reported and what to make of those reports and proposals afterwards between General Smith, who was in Sarajevo starting his tenure there, and the United Nations -- his superiors which were in Zagreb. General Smith, I think as history notes, was not afraid to draw a more clear line in the sand than some of his superiors were within the UN framework and that caused a certain degree of friction. So while I can say that certainly at the tactical levels that people like Colonel Karremans or General Nicolai or General Smith would have been reporting these facts up the United Nations chain of command, what I don't have a picture on is how accurately their concerns at Srebrenica and Sarajevo were being relayed to United Nations in New York by, I believe it was, the UN command in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: If I may have a followup question. Again, talking to you as a military person with experience not only in the former Yugoslavia but in other areas, would you say that the failure of the commanders on the ground in the former Yugoslavia to report the encirclement of the UNPROFOR soldiers, their disablement, was a failure on their part? To the soldiers especially who were put in harm's way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, what I would say is I am aware of what the military commanders do and did and what they reported. The problem that you have, particularly within the United Nations chain of command as it existed at the time, is that at some point above General Smith, the military commander, his superiors were United Nations diplomats. They were not soldiers. So again going back to the United Nations report, there is a major disconnect between what the soldiers are reporting and what they believe the proper remedies are versus what the diplomats and the politicians in the UN bureaucracy are seeing or are perceiving the situation to be. So I don't know that the military commanders weren't reporting up the chain of command. What is unclear to me, and I would again refer you back to the United Nations report, is at what level their view of the situation was being watered down or modified by their superiors for other reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I add a very small issue. I need a clarification to the transcript. On page -- you can't see it anymore, it disappeared from the screen. Page 20, line 24. I read from the transcript. Your answer was: "As I -- again, I recall from the United Nations report it was known in Sarajevo, it was known in Zagreb Zvornik Brigade, which was the headquarters for the entire operation dealing with Yugoslavia." I think there could be a little mistake or misunderstanding. Could you clarify this sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. When I said "Zagreb" -- I hope I didn't say "Zvornik Brigade," but Zagreb was the apparent headquarters for the United Nations forces dealing with the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. That was a necessary clarification. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you to the Judges and Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please answer this question: Is it possible that the UN headquarters in New York was not informed of the restrictions imposed on the UNPROFOR mandate in Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anything is possible. I mean, I'm kind of -- I suspect the answer that everyone is looking for is in that UN report. I just can't tell you off the top of my head at what point in time the UN leadership in New York would have been made aware of that or if they were. Again, I would refer you back to the UN report on that where I -- where I believe the answer is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Butler, I have to come back to you. I have read the Secretary-General's report that you are referring to which ultimately led to the establishment of this Tribunal to look for the truth, and it's through people like you that we hope, to the extent possible, that we can reach to the truth. So I come back to the last question which was: Is it possible, in the normal line of chain of command, whether it's military or in fact civil, that the events surrounding UNPROFOR were not communicated to the UN command in New York? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible. But given the fact that not only would one expect the United Nations to report that through their chain of command but that the Dutch government, since their forces were in Srebrenica, and they were receiving information directly from their units there, that if the Dutch felt that the UN wasn't receiving an accurate picture in the New York UN level, that the Dutch UN representatives would take it upon themselves, if instructed by the government, to inform the UN of just that. So there were two possible reporting mechanisms, at least, that would have allowed for the highest levels of the United Nations to be aware of those restrictions of movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you to Judge Nyambe and Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If that was the case, if it was possible that the UN headquarters in New York had not been informed, was it also possible that based on incomplete information about the situation in the field, they made decisions about the engagement of NATO forces against the VRS in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could just ask for a little more particularity because NATO forces in 1995 is very general and they may each have a different story each time it was used. If the general is speaking of something in particular, it would be very helpful. Otherwise, it's a vast area, as far as I know, NATO in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, can you help Mr. McCloskey to clarify that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, if before the events in Srebrenica NATO forces attacked the VRS forces, was it possible that this activity on their part was the result of inaccurate information about the situation in the field? Was it possible that they had incomplete information about the balance of forces? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my understanding, if you're talking about the NATO air-strikes in June of 1995, the trigger to that military activity was the withdrawal by the VRS of artillery from a monitoring area around Sarajevo, and since that artillery could no longer be monitored by an earlier agreement between the United Nations, the VRS, and the ABiH, that that was the trigger to the bombing campaign related to June of 1995. I don't know whether or not or how clear or how not clear that particular picture was in New York versus in Sarajevo or Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. If NATO forces were activated pursuant to requests from the UN Security Council against the VRS, does this mean that -- what does it mean, really? Was the UNPROFOR mandate in Bosnia to maintain peace or to impose peace?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UN mandate was peacekeeping and not peace enforcement, so you're correct there. And certainly while there was a supposedly separate chain of command between the United Nations forces and the NATO forces, it certainly blurs the line when you have that situation occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Tell us, was the use of weapons pursuant to requests from the United Nations a peacekeeping or a peace enforcement operation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure how they characterised that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We will now see what the testimony on this particular issue was by Mr. Rupert Smith and what his understanding of NATO activities in 1995 in Bosnia was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please call up D193, that's General Rupert Smith's statement. You can see page 1 here. Can we now show page 9, paragraph 5, of the statement by General Rupert Smith. Thank you, Aleksandar. It's page 9, paragraph 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It reads, and I'm quoting General Smith's words: "At the end of this series of meetings I had come to the conclusion that the Bosnian Serbs had concluded that further fighting was inevitable and that they had to reach some form of conclusion within the year. The eastern enclaves were too strong and the Bosnian Army within them constituted a clear threat, particularly as the VRS felt that they were likely to face attacks on multiple fronts." And there's the sentence you referred to: "In the enclaves the UN were being used as a shield by the Bosnians and a hostage by the Serbs. The intention of the Serbs appeared to be to force the UN into a position of abandoning the enclaves to enable the BSA to defeat or at least contain the Bosnian Army in Eastern Bosnia and to release vital manpower for other areas." This is my question: Were you aware of Mr. General Smith stating something like this? This was a conclusion drawn by him in March of 1995, and that's something you can glean from further up in the text. Do you believe that the Security Council was informed of this too or was the information concerning the combat readiness of the forces in the enclaves withheld from them? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first part of your question, I am aware of this. I have read this statement a number of times before. I believe that the particular paragraph that you discussed is the view that General Smith had at the time, and I believe it roughly correlates to the view that I have come to based on separate materials. As to your last question, I just -- I do not know if this particular information was transmitted all the way up to the Security Council in New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. It was -- it is for your sake and for the sake of the Trial Chamber that I should draw your attention to paragraph 2 on page 9 in Serbian, where Mr. Smith says -- and that's page 8, paragraph 2: "I met with Mladic at his request in a hotel in Vlasenica on my return from Srebrenica to Sarajevo." So I'm drawing your attention to the time-frame. So he went to Srebrenica, and on his return, on the 7th of March, he met up with Mladic and arrived at that conclusion, which was his general conclusion about the forces of the ABiH in the enclaves. This is my question: Is it possible that the UN Security Council did not receive General Smith's report about the situation in the safe areas and that he visited these areas, in fact, without the consent from the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This time I guess I will answer your second question first. As the commander on the ground, General Smith should and would have had all of the necessary authorities to visit any of the troops under his command. So I don't believe that he would have had to have asked for the United Nations Security Council's permission at any level to personally view the situation in enclaves or any other of the military units, the UN peacekeeping units, under his direction. So that would not have been required. Again, going to your first question, I don't know how far up the chain of command that the information or that these observations, these specific observations by General Smith would have been transmitted. So I mean, I know that he would have and should have reported these issues. They would have gone to his superiors in Zagreb. What I just don't have any clarity on is whether or not the UN command in Zagreb passed these reports verbatim to the UN Security Council or the UN -- actually, their intervening headquarters would be the Department of Peacekeeping Operations in New York, not necessarily the UN Security Council, or whether General Smith had the reporting ability and exercised it that he would report directly to the Department of Peacekeeping Operations in New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. In his statement - and I don't want to quote it in its entirety - Mr. Smith says that he met up with all the sides to see what the possibility was for maintaining the cessation of hostilities agreement which was in force between January and April of 1994 and he did that because the United Nations were looking into the possibilities for this agreement to be prolonged. He says that he was in meetings with civilian and military leaders on this particular issue. So let's look at the very next paragraph, which reads -- and that's page 9, and I'm quoting: "The meeting with General Mladic" -- I'm sorry. "The meeting with General Blaskic at the HVO headquarters in Posusje was held on the 8th of March."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you please give us the reference to the English page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English that's page 9, paragraph 4. Thank you. My apologies. Thank you, Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will quote again: "On the 8th of March, a meeting was held with General Blaskic at HVO headquarters in Posusje. The meeting was followed by a joint press statement for Croatian TV. The main areas for discussion were the cessation of hostilities agreement process, the UNPROFOR mandate in Croatia, federation military matters, and the military situation currently in Bosnia." And now, next he lists a meeting with Mr. Muratovic and states that he was in Zagreb on the 11th of March with Mr. Akashi. This is the following paragraph. The fifth paragraph lists his meeting with Muratovic; the sixth, with Mr. Akashi in Zagreb; and the seventh, the meeting with Mr. Akashi at Pale, et cetera. Let us see when -- this is what I quoted to you to see when exactly this happened. Now, this is my question for you: Did you review documents where you found that the BH Army violated the cessation of hostilities agreement and launched a comprehensive offensive on all the fronts? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just if -- if we could be made clear what year this report is referring to? He said 1994, which may be correct, but frankly, it's -- from what I see on the screen I can't tell and I'm not sure which year he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, could you clarify it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you to Mr. McCloskey for mentioning this issue. It has to do with 1995, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So I repeat my question: Did the BH Army violate the truce and the cessation of hostilities agreement that was in force in January through to May 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: By April and May of 1995 there was a series of military operations undertaken by both the ABiH 1st Corps in and around Sarajevo and by ABiH 2 Corps in north of the Tuzla area, so what I'm just not clear of is exactly when the scheduled date of the cease-fire was supposed to end or -- so I don't know whether it was technically a violation of the cease-fire, whether they jumped the gun early, or whether they waited for the cease-fire to expire and then militarily moved on. But I agree with your basic point, which is that by late April, early May of 1995, at least in the 1st and 2nd Corps areas, the ABiH did jump off to significant offensive military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Let's now look at page 9, paragraph 3, the last line. In English, that's page 9, paragraph 1, which reads: "The purpose of these meetings was to encourage the Bosnian government to recommit itself to the cessations of hostilities agreement and to inject new incentive to apply the agreement" -- or "comply with the agreement." This is my question: Can it be concluded, based on the statement by General Smith, that the Muslims did not comply with the cessations of hostilities agreement in the course of 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's page 9, the penultimate paragraph, the one that I quoted a moment ago, and I mean the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The last sentence of the penultimate paragraph. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sir, I mean, in that context, certainly the UN's interest was in maintaining any cease-fire because that, of course, kept down civilian casualties. Realistically, given the situation that the ABiH found itself in its own territory, that a lot of the territory it believed was theirs was, in fact, occupied by the VRS, I don't believe the ABiH was ever serious about a long-term cease-fire that was going to leave them in that particularly disadvantaged situation. So I suspect, at the end of the day, the answer was exactly what everyone thought it was going to be, which was that the Bosnian Muslim military forces were using the cease-fire as a means to resupply themselves, to reorganise their military forces, and then seek to go on the offensive in the early part of 1995, March/April, when the weather gave them the ability to go on these offensives, with the goal of trying to put the Army of Republika Srpska at a disadvantage. So in the broader context I agree with General Tolimir that the ABiH probably was never serious about maintaining a cease-fire that was going to go through the summer, you know, through May, June, July, and August of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the time for our break and we will resume then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Indeed, we must have our first break now and we will resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir. Please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, at the end of the last session you said that the BH Army never had a firm intention of honouring the cease-fire, the cessation of hostilities agreement. Did I understand this correctly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The transcript is slightly different, Mr. Tolimir. He said: "... I agree with General Tolimir that the ABiH probably was never serious about maintaining a cease-fire ..." This is a bit different. Therefore, I just wanted to have the correct version on the record. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In that case I don't need an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So you said "probably." Now, concerning that whole situation, my question is: With the agreement on the cessation of hostilities, did the VRS sign with the ABiH, the Croatian Army, and the representatives of the international community, such as the UNPROFOR commanders, an agreement that was a guarantee that the ABiH also undertook to honour?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We will also look at this agreement on the cessation of hostilities.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1011 is the document we need in e-court. Here it is. In English and in Serbian, page 1. I should like to ask for the last page to be shown, with the signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you see on that last page that it was signed by Alija Izetbegovic, Radovan Karadzic, Rasim Delic, and Kresimir Zubak and Vladimir Soljic on behalf of the Croats, and it was co-signed by Yasushi Akashi on behalf of the United Nations, and Michael Rose on behalf of the UNPROFOR command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do. Or it says "witnessed" by them not on behalf of them. But just the same, I see their signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the United Nations initiated and advocated this agreement on the cessation of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the origins of the particular cease-fire agreement or which side advocated it first. I just don't know the answer to that question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could we please look at Article 2. That's on page 1. I will quote: "The cessation of hostilities will be supervised and monitored by UNPROFOR through the establishment of joint commissions. A central joint commission shall be established under the chairmanship of the UNPROFOR, with initial meetings at the Sarajevo airport. And regional joint commissions shall also be established in permanent session as needed and as determined by the central joint commission." Paragraph 3: "Liaison officers will be exchanged between UNPROFOR and the parties by 15 January 1995 and afterwards where determined appropriate -- where deemed appropriate." Is it clear from this that UNPROFOR was the guarantor and the supervisor of this cessation of hostilities agreement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with your phrase "supervised and monitored" because that is what it states specifically in Article 2. I am not sure, contextually, whether that also means the guarantor of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In that case let us look at paragraph 4. It says: "Cessation of hostilities will include the following measures: "A. Separation of forces in conflict to mutually agreed positions and the positioning of UNPROFOR forces for observation and monitoring to include interpositioning." My question is: Did the UNPROFOR deploy its forces between the parties in conflict in order to enforce this agreement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am trying to picture back to Sarajevo, at least, where the UN, if they ever actually managed to achieve that, where they were able to put their forces or interpose them between the VRS and the ABiH. I don't know if that ever happened. If it did, it didn't happen to a large degree simply because, militarily, there was a lot of resistance to the idea of giving up certain key terrain features that had been hard fought over to a UN force that might then turn them over to the other side. So there are a number of occasions that I'm aware of where there was serious contention between the VRS, the UN, and the ABiH over [Realtime transcript read in error "other"] the withdrawal of certain military units or positions because of their perceived strategic value at a certain area. So if it did occur, I don't believe it occurred in large numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, did you say "over the withdrawal" or "other the withdrawal."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Over the withdrawal, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. It relates to line 21 of page 35. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Did you come across a UN document where it says that in Sarajevo, during separation, the Serbs handed over the Vrbanja bridge to UNPROFOR, which was followed by an incident when the Serbs wanted to recover Vrbanja bridge into their control. Rupert Smith talks about it in his statement. Have you read that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am generally aware of the bridge incident, as it's described, but I do not know of the specific details of when the bridge was supposed to be turned over and by which parties to whom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, first of all, good afternoon to everyone. On page 36, line 10, the name of the bridge is not recorded correctly. The bridge is called Vrbanja, V-r-b-a-n-j-a.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, if the river separated Muslims and Serbs, and the Serbs and Muslims controlled parts of the bridge, each on their own side, does it mean that the bridge was not, in fact, controlled by the Serbs once the bridge was handed over? Let's look at what Mr. Rupert Smith says about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you put a question to the witness. Are you expecting an answer?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked whether the witness has read the statement of General Rupert Smith concerning the problem of the Vrbanja bridge, because he said he was not sure there was a separation of forces in Sarajevo and that was done precisely in order to separate forces. That's what I asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies, I assumed we were going to go to that part of the statement. I don't recall offhand what General Smith said or did not say about that. I would suggest we go to the statement on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the electronic courtroom to display D193. When we see the first page, let's see also page 15 of that statement in English. It's the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: He says: "On the 27 May, Bosnian Serb troops disguised as French soldiers seized a French position at Vrbanja bridge in Sarajevo, killing two French soldiers and taking 11 prisoner. The French counter-attacked, killing four Serb troops and taking six prisoners. At roughly the same time, the Bosnian Serbs took 30 UNPROFOR personnel hostage with their vehicles and equipment from the Gorazde area." This was written by Mr. Smith. My question is: Were the French able to hold any features in Sarajevo unless these had been handed over by the warring parties, and was it their job to hold positions between the warring parties and to separate them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the broad mandate, where the UN forces were placed and what territory they held was ultimately at the discretion of the various warring parties. It was a peacekeeping mission, not a peace enforcement one. For example, the UN didn't occupy the Sarajevo airport. It was permitted to use that by the various warring parties for various purposes. So the positions and the check-points that were maintained by the United Nations were done so with the consent of the warring parties. If the warring parties did not consent to that, then the UN would not have been able to maintain those positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. You just mentioned the Sarajevo airport. Do you know which one of the warring parties held the Sarajevo airport before it was handed over to UNPROFOR? Have you found that in any of the documents you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that the airport was initially held by the Yugoslav National Army military forces that were there at the beginning of the conflict. I believe they are the ones who turned it over to the -- I believe they are the ones who turned it over to the UN forces at the very beginning of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. We'll show you that agreement and you will see that it was handed over by Mr. Koljevic. But that's not the purpose of my question. My purpose was to tell you that in Sarajevo there also occurred a separation of forces at points such as Vrbanja bridge, the airport and other points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I am going to object to that style. If he wants to impeach the witness on a particular point that he thinks is important, he should do it at the time that he brings it up, not make a comment contradicting the witness and -- for some later time. I mean, if he's got something to contradict the witness, he should bring it up and use it. Otherwise, he's just testifying and he knows that he shouldn't be doing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, the way the last sentence was formulated is problematic. "My purpose is to tell you that," and then it's not properly recorded. You shouldn't tell him. You should ask him about his experience and his knowledge. Please continue your interrogation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. It is not my intention to make the witness uncomfortable. I am just speaking of facts that I am going to show him in documents, such as this Vrbanja bridge incident. So I'm not going to insist on getting an answer on these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let me ask this: Did UNPROFOR representatives hand over to the VRS the positions they had received from them during the separation forces in areas between the ABiH and VRS? If you know that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're talking about Sarajevo, then I don't know the answer to that. That was not a specific focus on what my military analysis was doing on -- on the day-to-day with respect to what was going on with Sarajevo, so I don't know the details of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know any details concerning Srebrenica? Did Muslims did out of the Srebrenica demilitarised zone in order to get more advantageous positions and to mount attacks against VRS units?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to 1995, I would characterise most of the military operations by the ABiH out of the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa more along the lines of raids. Go out, launch a specific attack against a discrete target, achieve those objectives, and then fall back into the enclaves. They did not have the military power necessary to go out of the enclaves, generally, and hold territory in the face of a sustained VRS counterattack.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let us look at the situation in Srebrenica on the 13th of July, discussed by Mr. Smith in his statement. It's page 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 3 in Serbian. Page 16 in Serbian, last paragraph. It's the 3rd paragraph in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let me quote it, then you will maybe find it more easily. "Until 13 July, I believed the Muslims had managed to escape, but whether successfully or not I didn't know. The BH Army told me nothing about it." And before that he says they had occasionally left the enclave and taken up certain positions. My question is: Have you read any documents, any UNPROFOR reports saying that Muslims in the enclaves went out of the enclaves, across the front line, and took up positions in the territory held by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, I am still not finding the paragraph that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I am in the same position. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it's the second half of the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I've read the paragraph. Now what was your question again, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The question was, I quote: "Have you read any documents, any UNPROFOR reports saying that Muslims in the enclaves went out across the front line and took up positions by the territory held by the VRS?" That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are we talking in the period before the fall of Srebrenica or afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What about before the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I testified earlier, before the fall of Srebrenica, the military operations conducted by the ABiH were in the series of raids, where they would go out, do discrete military operations, and then fall back into the enclave. It was not a goal of holding territory, so to speak, and defending that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, does that mean that they had to go across the front lines to get behind the lines of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, as you're aware, despite the military forces that were around the enclaves from the VRS, there was never a cohesive series of lines. There were a number of gaps between various military units. So I suspect that the tactic that was used was not necessarily to breach through where the military positions were, but it was to essentially exploit the gaps in the lines and to go around those military positions to get behind the VRS units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Do you know that part of the agreement we read envisaged the deployment of liaison officers from one territory to the other? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe in the agreement that was the prior exhibit, the phrase was that there would be liaison officers and other regional commissions as deemed necessary or as determined necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Let me tell you that General Smith mentions this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at page 11, the last paragraph of his statement, the version in Serbian -- or, rather, it's paragraph 3 of his statement in Serbian. Page 11. And that is page 11, the first three paragraphs in English. Thank you, Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "I informed Dr. Karadzic that as I could no longer guarantee the safety of the Bosnian Serb liaison officers in Gornji Vakuf, I intended to return them. I delivered a letter to this effect. Karadzic agreed to this, and the BSA liaison officers were returned to the Bosnian Serb Army at 1900 hours that evening." This is my question: A warring party, in this case the Muslims, did they not give a clear indication of violating the cessation of hostilities agreement by this and that they returned the liaison officers to the territory of Republika Srpska? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular document just mentions one instance at Gornji Vakuf. I don't know whether this applies to all of them or not, and without knowing any of the context around that, I am just not able to answer the question as whether or not this should be an indicator that they were going to violate the cease-fire. It's just not enough information to go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me avoid testifying and giving information. It is not my purpose. What I would like is to show you elements of the agreement that were violated. This is what I tried to do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at page 10, the last paragraph of the statement by General Rupert Smith where he speaks about the offensive activities of the Bosnian Muslims. Page 10, paragraph 3, and page 9, paragraph 1, clearly indicates that this was on the 13th of March. All these events happened on the 11th, 12th, and 13th of March, as expressed in Mr. Smith's statement. And page 9, the last paragraph clearly indicates that it was the 13th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which page in English?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 9, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says: "On the 13th of March ..." Let's move to page 10 now, please. I was showing you this to indicate the time-frame only. We don't want to go through the entire statement. Let's look at the last paragraph of page 10 in Serbian, which is paragraph 3 of page 10 in English, which reads: "Matters continued to deteriorate during the following week when the Bosnian Army mounted an offensive in two directions claiming that it was designed to relieve pressure on Bihac. One attack on the Vlasic feature was ultimately successful, but the attack on the Majevica hills from Tuzla was not."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is my question: Four locations are referred to here. Namely, Bihac; Vlasic, near Travnik; Majevica, on the border between Republika Srpska and the Federation, near Tuzla; and the offensive out of Tuzla in the direction of the borders of Republika Srpska. Is that not the case, that these four locations are mentioned here? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, you're correct. It mentions those four locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's see what General Smith has to say further down. "I took the view that the Bosnian government had no intention of extending the cessation of hostilities agreement beyond the end of April." He goes on to say: "On the 22nd of March, I met with Dr. Ganic, Mr. Muratovic and General Hajrulahovic. I was accompanied by Mr. Aguilar. The purpose of the meeting was to assess the political stance of the Bosnian government in relation to the cessation of hostilities agreement following the Bosnian offensive in the Tuzla area. "On the 23rd of March, I met with General Delic in order to gain a clearer understanding of the Tuzla and Travnik areas and assess the potential for maintaining the cease-fire in Bosnia." This is my question: Does it not follow clearly from this portion of General Smith's statement that, in March, the Muslim army did not want to honour the cessation of hostilities agreement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean this is General Smith's interpretation of events that were occurring on the ground at the time. And again, as I've testified before, within the context of what was happening on the ground, how much territory the VRS controlled versus the ABiH, I don't believe that politically there was a will to maintain the cease-fire by the Bosnian government at the time. It would have been politically unfavourable for them to do so, and militarily, they would not have been able to sustain those line indefinitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this not constitute a violation of the cessation of hostilities agreement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess in a technical sense it would constitute a violation. If -- when one party goes over to the offence, again, depending on the specifics of the agreement, you're -- you're violating the cease-fire by taking offensive action. That would be a technical violation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move to the next page, which is page 12 in Serbian. The last paragraph. And the corresponding page in English is 12, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I quote: "Consultations with the Bosnian government included meetings with Silajdzic, Muratovic, Ganic, and Sacirbey. The Bosnians were quite clear that an extension of the cessation of hostilities agreement was not in their interest, and they took the opportunity again to criticise the weak and contradictory UNPROFOR mandates and the strangulation of Sarajevo by the Bosnian Serbs." Can you perhaps tell the Trial Chamber what the distance is between Sarajevo and the locations we mentioned earlier, Majevica, Vlasic, Tuzla, in order for them to have an understanding of it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a kilometre basis. They are not in the Sarajevo area is what I can say. They are in different areas of the country that are outside of the normal area that you would consider part of Sarajevo. So they are not related in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move on to the next page. In Serbian, that's page 12, paragraph 1, the last sentence of the paragraph. That's page 12 in English, paragraph 3 from the bottom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I quote the last sentence of that paragraph. There is a reference to a meeting between Karadzic and Smith, and it is stated here: "Again he offered a permanent cease-fire on condition that they were treated equally in relation to the Bosnians and that sanctions against themselves were lifted." He said that: "If the international community treated the Serbs like beasts in a cage, then that is how they would behave." Did General Smith state in this statement in the Serbs had agreed to a permanent cessation of hostilities, unlike the Muslims, who refused to do so and violated the cessation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this paragraph he does reflect that that is what -- he sources that back to President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As a military analyst, tell us this: If a warring party agrees to a cessation of hostilities and the other does not, which of the two parties would be deemed responsible for the continuation of a war? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If only life were that simple. The problem that you have to look at when you look at this in context is that, frankly, from November of 1992 onwards, the Bosnian Serbs were, for the most part, looking to end hostilities. Their position was that they had achieved all of their territorial gains, they had unified their population group in areas that they wanted under their contiguous control, but the other side of the party didn't. The Bosnian Muslim government particularly was significantly disadvantaged by the military situation on the ground and the political one. That was inherent in that. So the fact that the side -- or one party of the conflict, which is achieving all of their war aims and has achieved them in their mind, wants to end hostilities doesn't make it necessarily the fault of the other party which is on the losing end of that stick to come to peace because it's not advantageous for them. In this particular context, militarily neither side could administer the knockout blow; however, neither side could sue for peace under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Tell us, if both parties signed a cessation of hostilities agreement and one of the sides wishes to continue complying with it whereas the other does not, which of the two would be responsible for the continuing war? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would be -- the side that continued to conduct military operations would be technically in violation of the cease-fire. So whether being in technical violation of the cease-fire equates to being at fault for the continuation of the war is a harder question. Again, within the context of what was happening on the ground, I believe that the ABiH engaged in this cease-fire for the tactical purpose of being able to re-equip and resupply and retrain their military forces.
