I don't believe they ever had the position was that the cease-fire and the military positions that they possessed when they agreed to it in late 1994 -- in November or December of 1994 and in early January of 1995, were the military positions that they planned to end the conflict on. I don't believe that they believed that those positions, in December of 1994 and January of 1995, would have left them with a viable state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I don't see in the body of your answer the answer to the question, which was: "If both parties signed a cessation of hostilities agreement and one of the sides wishes to continue complying with it whereas the other does not, which of the two would be responsible for the continuation of the war?" Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rather than in the abstract, technically let's just say what it is. The Bosnian Muslim side was not willing to live with the cease-fire beyond a certain point when they believed that they could achieve their objectives militarily. That point started in March of 1995 with the resumption of large-scale military operations in various locations. The cease-fire, it was just what it was. It was a temporary agreement to stop military conflict. It was not a precursor, and I don't believe the Bosnian Muslims ever viewed it to be the pre-cursor to a permanent peace agreement. So when the conflict began again in earnest in March of 1995 by the offensives in 1st and 2nd Corps area, they were done so by the Bosnian Muslims for their purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Which were the purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Their purpose was primarily to regain territory that they believed was theirs. Particularly with respect to Sarajevo, when you look at where the Bosnian Serb and Bosnian Muslim military positions were and the stranglehold that the Bosnian Serbs had over the city, there should be no question that that situation would -- could somehow continue in a non-conflict -- or in a post-conflict stage. That would not have left the Bosnian Muslim side with a viable capital, let alone a viable country. So their purpose was the same purpose that they had since November of 1992, which was to continue military activities against primarily the Bosnian Serbs for the purpose of recapturing or regaining territory that they believed was rightfully theirs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, do you know that the Muslims fought in Bosnia both the Serbs and the Croats before the cessation of hostilities? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that during the cessation of hostilities an agreement was signed between the Muslims and the Croats about the establishment of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and a cessation of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say "cessation of hostilities," you're referring to the cessation of hostilities between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims; correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Butler. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I am aware of that, sir. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know who it was who imposed the cessation of hostilities agreement in Bosnia? Did it come about spontaneously among the warring parties or was it imposed by someone?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we talking about the one between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims again?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now we have moved on to the comprehensive cessation of hostilities agreement in Bosnia. Was it imposed by anyone, and if so, by whom?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's see what General Smith has to say about it in his statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 11, paragraph 2 in Serbian, and we will move on to paragraph 3. As for paragraph 2, we are only interested in the date. It's page 10 in English, the penultimate paragraph, as well as the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It reads: "On the 5th of April, I met privately with Dr. Karadzic at a hotel near Pale." So he's referring to the 5th of April during his term of office in 1995. I referred you to this paragraph merely for the date. In the subsequent paragraph he speaks of the substance of the meeting and says: "Karadzic took the opportunity to deliver a message to me in the knowledge that I would pass it on through the UN chain of command. The message was that the Bosnian Serbs had decided that the cessation of hostilities agreement had failed and that the Bosnian Serbs felt that they had been let down by the former US President Carter, the United Nations, and the international community." This is my question for you: Does it follow from this who was it who exerted pressure on the Serbs to agree to the cessation of hostilities agreement during the time when the Muslims were fighting both the Serbs and the Croats? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether this particular phrase is meant to imply that the former President Carter, the UN, and the international community imposed the agreement or whether President Karadzic is reflecting his disappointment because they had not been more forceful in trying to keep the agreement. So I don't know that I can answer your particular question there. Also with respect to your last comment, "the Muslims were fighting both the Serbs and the Croats," I am not aware that that was happening as late as April of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To bring clarity to this, let's look at page 19 of the statement of Mr. Smith. Paragraph 5 in Serbian, and in English it's page 18, the penultimate paragraph. Thank you, Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I quote: "On the 23rd of July, on my way back from London, I met with Mr. Sacirbey at Split airport. The meeting was at Sacirbey's request and followed the meeting and the Split agreement between Bosnian, Croatian, and Federation ministers. Sacirbey explained this agreement. We also discussed the situation in Zepa, the fighting in Bihac, the army of the RSK offensive, and the arrangements for the rapid reaction force." Can you tell on the basis of this reference to 1995 that this was following the cessation of hostilities agreement when the so-called Split declaration was signed by the Croats and the Muslims? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. That helped clarify it for me, because I thought in your prior question you were referencing the Bosnian Croats and Muslims. I didn't realise that you were discussing the actual Republic of Croatia in that context. So I am clear on that, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Since we are now clear on that, can you tell us, as a military analyst, did the Muslims violate the cessation of hostilities agreement because they believed that they had created the necessary conditions for contiguous territory, for linking up with the enclaves, and liberating Sarajevo? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if all of those conditions are met, but they violated -- or they basically terminated the cease-fire and initiated or reinitiated hostilities against Bosnian Serb military forces because they believed that militarily they could defeat them and to achieve the territorial aims that they were looking for. Liberating Sarajevo or breaking through the VRS siege lines that were there was one part of them. Enclaves were another part of the them, but there were territorial aspects to it as well that were even beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, did the enclaves then constitute a great problem in the territory of Republika Srpska because they mounted attacks against civilians at that same time that we are discussing, after the cessation of hostilities agreement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were a problem in the sense that, yes, they did target civilians coming out -- or military forces coming out of the enclaves did target civilians or civilian objects. But within the framework of what the larger levels of the VRS was looking at, and again as I discussed in my report, along this same time-frame, the VRS, just as the Bosnian Muslim military forces are seeing themselves growing stronger every day, politically with their alliance with the Bosnian Croats and later with Croatia, the Bosnian Serbs see themselves weakening every day. The Bosnian Serbs as early as March and April of 1995 were recognising the fact that 1995 would be the decisive year of the war for them. They were running to the end of their tether with respect to manpower, military equipment, so going back to well prior testimony, the military forces that were tied down around the enclaves were believed by General Mladic and the Army of Republika Srpska being squandered, if you will, when they could be used more profitably in other areas of the battle-field for the Republika Srpska. And, in fact, when one looks at what happens starting in August of 1995 with Croatian Operation Storm, in part, you know, they are successful because they are able to generate -- or I should make it clear that the Republic of Croatia is successful, because it's able to generate superior military force on those areas of the battle-fields that it needed to while large components of the VRS are still tied down dealing with the issues related to the eastern enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. You have now clarified this problem in Krajina and Croatia. You probably meant the western part of Republika Srpska. My question is: Did Serbs rightfully demand the demilitarisation of these areas in keeping with the agreement if the Muslims were attacking behind Serb lines from the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, in the sense that the cease-fire agreement -- and again using Srebrenica as an example, the cease-fire agreement did call for the forces to be demilitarised inside the enclaves, and it was recognised by the local Bosnian Serb military forces that they were not demilitarised and that the UN was not meaningfully enforcing the demilitarisation. So the Serbs did frequently raise that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Do you know that Serbs also raised it officially at meetings with UNPROFOR? Do you know this from the documents you've seen?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware, generally, that the VRS did complain about it. I am not sure off the top of my head which documents would illustrate that, but I agree that on many occasions the VRS military leadership raised the issue of the failure of the United Nations to demilitarise forces inside, specifically, the Zepa and Srebrenica enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Let me try to assist you by showing you the statement of Mr. Smith, page 13, last paragraph, where you can see that this issue was raised officially more than once.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at page 13. It's the fourth paragraph in English. Thank you, Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Quote: "On my return on the 21st May, I had a further private meeting with Dr. Karadzic. The discussion covered the future of UNPROFOR and in particular the UN presence in the eastern enclaves as well as the stabilisation process after the recent hostilities in Sarajevo." I stress this covered the future of UNPROFOR. "Karadzic confirmed that the Bosnian Serbs had effectively withdrawn consent for the UN operation stating that he had no belief in the impartiality, efficiency, and credibility of the UN. On the issue of the enclaves he said, 'They are a time bomb about to explode.' He maintained that the UN should get out but that UNHCR would be safe to remain. UNPROFOR presence, he stated, was welcome only if the enclaves were demilitarised and became safe areas for the population." My question is: In this specific case did the Serbs, the president of the Bosnian Serbs, make it clear to UNPROFOR commander that the UNPROFOR would not be welcome to stay there unless the Muslims stopped attacking from these enclaves and the enclaves were to be demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it specifically says is that UNPROFOR has no credibility in this respect anymore because it has not demilitarised the particular enclaves and that their presence would be welcome only if the enclaves weren't demilitarised. I take it from your comment that obviously if they are demilitarised, then the attacks would stop, but I mean, just to be clear, it does not specifically say that's not why they are welcome. It makes it clear that President Karadzic is upset about the fact that his position was that the UN never effectively demilitarised the enclaves and, as a result, they are no longer a credible peacekeeping force there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I quoted a moment ago the words of Mr. Karadzic to Mr. Smith, and Mr. Smith repeated it when he gave a statement to this OTP. But I don't mind if you look at it differently. My question is: Do you find it normal, as a military expert, that demilitarised area be full of troops and weapons and mount attacks against the side which granted it the status of a demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From a military perspective a demilitarised zone is supposed to be just that. It is supposed to be demilitarised for a purpose, and when one party demilitarises an area, that area is afforded the protections of a civilian or open area. Sadly, not only in the conflict in Bosnia but in many areas globally, apparently the new normal is that demilitarised areas are not effectively demilitarised and, as a result, combat activity continues to occur from it. It's not supposed to be that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. This is an area that was controlled by UN forces. So I'm asking you, was the entire international community supposed to be involved in their demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think such a broad -- "this area is controlled by UNPROFOR forces," what area has been controlled by UNPROFOR forces?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, if you want to have a precise answer you should put a precise question to the witness. Could you clarify it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank Mr. McCloskey, and I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since the Srebrenica area was controlled by UN forces called UNPROFOR, were they supposed to involve the entire international community in the demilitarisation of this area that they were supposed to control? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several different answers to that question. The first one is, I guess from a United Nations perspective, they are not sure, and when I say "them," I mean the Dutch Battalion, they are not sure they ever controlled the enclave. They are certainly not sure if that was ever their mission to do it. The whole context of the United Nations' own evaluation of the Srebrenica enclave is full of -- is full of assertions about the fact that they were unclear themselves at both the political level in New York at the department of peacekeeping and in Bosnia exactly what the mission and the roles of the forces inside the enclave were supposed to be. Whether they were there as merely a presence, which in effect was not much, or whether they were there to enforce a cease-fire, or whether they were there to enforce the demilitarisation of both parties or, in this case, of the Bosnia Muslim party. The problem in answering your question directly is the -- the problem that I have is that when the United Nations themselves, as evidenced in their own report, isn't clear on what their own political objectives are with respect to their presence in the enclave, that lack of clarity travelled all the way down the military chain of command so, ultimately, the military commanders of the various Dutch battalions that cycled through there themselves weren't clear exactly what their mission was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. And did they know which agreement they were implementing?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at D21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the meantime Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I am not quite sure whether I have a question or -- I'm a bit confused by the last answer by Mr. Butler. I thought there was a specific UN resolution describing what the mandate of UNPROFOR was, no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a specific resolution, I agree. However, one cannot escape the reality that UN resolutions are written very broadly and they do not readily translate themselves into military missions. I cite as an example, the recent UN mandate to protect civilians in Libya was not viewed by many of the people who voted for that mandate as an opening for NATO to engage in a bombing campaign in that country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to invite you to refrain from testifying about Libya. You should come back to this specific question by Judge Nyambe about the mandate of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, and I only do it as a point of example. I mean, the UN, in their report, was very -- the one thing that they were clear about was that at the political levels they didn't know what the mandate meant with respect to being in the enclaves. As you will recall, it was not a United Nations Security Council decision to declare Srebrenica a safe area. It was an after-the-fact ratification of a declaration and a commitment made by General Morillon. I suspect that had they to do it over again, they would have tried to provide General Morillon with more specific guidance about what he was or was not authorised to declare. Of course, you can't go back in history and fix that. In a perfect world, you could say and make the argument that the UN had the mission of demilitarising the safe area and that the Dutch military forces -- or first the Canadian military forces and later the Dutch would then consequentially have the mission of forcing the demilitarisation of that area. And if they could not or did not believe that forcing it was their job, they withdraw. But it's more than just a military problem. The phrases were used generally. First the Canadians and later the Dutch did not see it as their mission to enforce a cease-fire and to force compliance at the force of -- at the point of a gun, if necessary. And the UN, for its part, didn't see that it was going to be in a position to either make national contingents risk their soldiers' life to enforce that, and at the other side, they didn't see that it was in their interest to actually pull their military forces out completely and have no presence there. It is a particularly confusing situation and it is a particularly frustrating situation for military commanders who are used to very concrete mission orders and objectives from their national commands. I am not sure that the answer I am giving you helps to clarify the situation. I don't know that any answer could actually clarify it, given the confusion that the United Nations themselves at all levels of command had with respect to what they were supposed to be doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, I thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, indeed. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, here we see the agreement on the demilitarisation of Srebrenica and Zepa concluded between Lieutenant General Ratko Mladic and General Sefer Halilovic on the 8th of May, 1993. It says exactly what Judge Nyambe asked about. It says: "Confirming Resolution 824 of the Security Council in which it is declared that the towns of Zepa and Srebrenica and their surroundings should be treated as safe areas by all the parties concerned and should be free from armed attacks and from any other hostile act." Now, does this say that the Security Council dictated what Srebrenica and Zepa should look like?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it says is, and again it is a perfect illustration of the problem, that it declares them to be safe areas and to be treated by all parties as such. What it doesn't say is who is going to enforce this decision if one of the parties does not comply and how that enforcement will take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at section 1 of this agreement. It says: "To demilitarise the areas of Srebrenica and Zepa. "The demilitarised areas will include the area within the current lines of conflict." Following consultations: "The precise boundaries will be marked by the UNPROFOR commander, and the demilitarised zone shall be marked on the ground by UNPROFOR by means of boards on which it is stated in English, Serbian and Bosnian, written in Cyrillic and Latin, as follows: "Demilitarised zone."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "Any military operation is strictly forbidden (Article 60, protocol 1, additional to the Geneva Conventions)." Does this say clearly who is to designate the boundaries of the demilitarised area on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document says -- at least the English language one says it clearly, and I'm hoping this isn't an issue with translation, but it specifically notes that: "The precise boundaries will be marked by the UNPROFOR commander on the ground after consultations." I assume in this context the consultations they are talking about are between the Bosnian Muslim and the Bosnian Serb sides. And then: "At a later stage the contracting parties can agree, verbally or in writing, to enlarge the demilitarised zone." As you are aware, all the way through to the beginning of the military operation in July 1995, both the Bosnian Muslim side and the Bosnian Serb side disagreed as to what the demarcated boundaries of the enclave would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Would you please look at paragraph 3, with the leave of the Trial Chamber, or perhaps we should do it after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We should indeed do that after the break. We must have the second break now and we will resume quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, we left off dealing with Article 3, which reads: "Every military or paramilitary unit will have either to withdraw from the demilitarised zone or submit/hand-over their weapons. Ammunition, mines, explosives, and combat supplies in the demilitarised zones will be handed over/submitted to UNPROFOR. After submission/hand-over of all weapons, ammunition, mines, and combat supplies in the demilitarised zones, the contracting parties will declare that the demilitarisation is complete. Submitting/hand-over will be completed in Srebrenica by the 10th of May and in Zepa by the 12th of May. Submitting/hand-over of weapons will be observed by a team of officers from both sides together with UNPROFOR officers who will arrange the places where the hand-over will be done." And one more line from Article 4: "UNPROFOR shall take the handed over/submitted weapons into custody." And ammunition. This is my question: Article 4, does it not define the UNPROFOR mandate in very precise terms in relation to the demilitarised zone? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to your question is that that particular question itself raises the entire crux of the issue related to the UN forces in Srebrenica and this particular cease-fire agreement. The Bosnian Serb side believed that these particular -- Article 3 and Article 4 gave the United Nations forces in Srebrenica the mandate and mission to enforce the cease-fire. The broader United Nations didn't agree with that in that context. Their view was that the contracting parties would turnover the weapons, the United Nations would monitor those weapons' containment areas, but they did not view it as their role to take the next step, which was to enforce compliance with this agreement in particular cases where particularly the Bosnian Muslims did not turnover all their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for this interpretation, Mr. Butler. Based on the provisions of the agreement, were they supposed to turnover all of their weapons to UNPROFOR? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Article 3 is very specific. It specifically says: "All weapons, ammunition, and mines."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now look at Article 5: "UNPROFOR shall control the demilitarised zone. "To be able to implement this, an UNPROFOR unit and United Nations Military Observers with sufficient strength to control the area shall be present in the demilitarised zone. Until the contracting parties agree otherwise, the UNPROFOR strength shall be of at least a company group with command and supplying elements in each demilitarised zone. "In order to be able to resupply and rotate the unit, UNPROFOR shall have freedom of movement to and from the demilitarised zone." This is my question: In view of Article 5, was UNPROFOR supposed to furnish the forces which would make sure that the area is demilitarised and which would provide units of a company level and that they would have their companies complete with the respective commands? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 5 specifies the minimum size will be a company. And, in fact, the force that was initially in Srebrenica was a Canadian infantry company. Later, it was increased to a battalion-level-sized force, a larger force because all the parties, for the most part, didn't think that a mere company could control the size of the area. So Article 5 did set the framework for the size of the UN force that was believed to be sufficient to control the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Pursuant to the Security Council resolution, was UNPROFOR able to provide sufficient forces for the demilitarised zone or was the situation, in fact, such that they would say that they were unable to control a demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it started as a company level and that was increased later on to a battalion-level force. Whether or not a battalion, or even as the Dutch a reinforced battalion, had the ability to control effectively an area that big is always going to be a matter of dispute. That's an awful lot of territory for a battalion to control. So while the UN's job was to go in there and control that particular area, again, given the ambiguity of what the phrase "control" meant in the context, it was initially believed that a battalion was enough. In fact, a battalion probably was too little.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, do the United Nations normally operate on the principle of one soldier to one soldier, one civilian to one civilian, or do they normally assess the situation as to how they would be able to demilitarised an area -- demilitarise an area? And do they, at that level, define the strength of the forces that are to demilitarise a zone, or is that left to those who are, in fact, present on the ground with the purpose of demilitarising an area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the reality is that, one, there is no United Nations principle; and two, the cold, hard fact of the situation is that there is no United Nations army either. The United Nations is completely dependent on donor military -- or donor countries to allow their military forces to be used under a UN mandate. One of the -- again, referring back to the UN report on this issue, one of the underlying themes that is also part of that report is that even after declaring these various areas safe areas, there was a distinct reluctance by a number of countries that had loaned forces to the United Nations for the mission in Bosnia to actually then agree that their military units can be used inside of these enclaves. It was seen as being particularly -- having some particular risk to it. So as a result, there was a bit of an a shuffle and a serious amount of diplomatic work involved at the UN trying to come up with the adequate number of forces for the safe areas. Again, if I recall the UN report correctly, the UN at some point in time came up with a number of how many military forces it thought it needed to adequately enforce the safe areas. And again, if I recall correctly, the forces that donor countries made available were significantly less than what the UN thought it needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. If the party which designates an area demilitarised is going about that business, is it not the obligation of the United Nations to state whether they are able to do that or not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: One would think that if you're going to make that obligation that you're going to be able to back up that obligation. In fact, again, going to the situation with Srebrenica, the UN Security Council was reacting to events that had already occurred on the ground with the establishment of the Srebrenica safe area. It wasn't coming up with its own plan independently. So to some degree, had it to do themselves, the United Nations Security Council may never have come up with this whole safe area idea, but they were reacting to a decision on the ground already made by General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at D193 again, page 9. That's the statement by General Smith, who was UNPROFOR commander at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: At page 9, paragraph 2, he states as follows -- that's page 8 in English, the penultimate paragraph. I quote: "On the 7th of March, upon my return, I met up with Mladic." Rather than me reading the whole paragraph, let me just read the important line: "The third most important issue that was discussed was the demilitarisation of the safe areas of Gorazde, Srebrenica, and Zepa. On the issue of Srebrenica, Mladic asked that I should order the withdrawal of all the UNPROFOR forces from the confrontation line south-east of Zepa. He maintained that the movement of observer missions of UNPROFOR in this area made it possible for the Bosnians to occupy the area and a very important road that was under the control of the Serbs. I refused to do so and explained that it was my duty to observe the confrontation line." This is my question: If the side which conferred upon Srebrenica the status of demilitarised area, if it's asking to be withdrawn because its unable to control the area, under the Geneva Conventions, is the UNPROFOR commander able to say simply that he is unable to do so or should he report that back to the authority that empowered him to be there to begin with?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, with respect, I am not sure what, if anything, the Geneva Conventions have to do with that. What I would say - and again, not wanting to put words in General Smith's mouth - the fact is that General Smith was the UN commander on the ground and would not make -- or not make a commitment, but would not basically lay out what his position were in that regard unless he believed that it was the position of his superiors and that they would support his decision on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Butler, I said in keeping with the Geneva Conventions, because each and every Geneva Convention envisages the status of a demilitarised zone which can be conferred upon a given area. You were able to see here a reference to Article 60 of the Geneva Conventions in that very agreement we were reading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 1D1005. That's Protocol 1 of the Geneva Convention. 1D1005, thank you. Article 60. At page 20 in English and 26 in Serbian. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree with the context of -- that it mentions the Geneva Conventions. Where I take issue is the fact that while those particular articles will deal with what are -- what is a safe area and how it's established, I mean, the same thing applies. I mean, the Geneva Conventions don't have a particular enforcement mechanism. For these provisions to work, it requires the willingness of both parties to agree to follow the concepts. So whether or not General Smith believes that his forces there are enforcing a cease-fire or keeping warring parties apart, and the decisions that General Smith takes in that regard are not enforceable by the Geneva Conventions is the point that I'm trying to make. And that's why I say I don't see how one has to do with the other. In General Smith's decisions as to where he's going to maintain forces in an effort to try and comply with the cease-fire agreement is dictated by what his superiors in the United Nations are telling him, not by the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You've started answering before I put my question to you. Let's now look at item 1 of Article 60: "It is prohibited for the parties to the conflict to extend their military operations to zones on which they have conferred by agreement the status of demilitarised zone if such extension is contrary to the terms of this agreement." This is my question: Was it contrary to the provisions of the agreement for the Muslims from the demilitarised zones to carry out sabotage actions within Republika Srpska? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, not being an international law expert but just being a military analyst, I mean the common-sense answer is that if you were conducting military operations out of a demilitarised area, it is no longer demilitarised, or at least the real estate that you are conducting your operations off of. You open yourself up to military attack or retaliation in that effect by your armed enemy. Now, whether or not conducting one or three or five military attacks out of the safe area invalidates an entire safe area is a question I am not capable of answering.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's look at paragraph 7 of this same article, which continues on the following page. I am quoting item 7 of Article 60: "If one of the parties to the conflict commits a material breach of the provisions of paragraphs 3 or 6, the other party shall be released from its obligations under the agreement conferring upon the zone the status of demilitarised zone. In such an eventuality, the zone allows its status but shall continue to enjoy the protection provided by the other provisions of this Protocol and the other rules of international law applicable in armed conflict." This is my question: If the Muslim side violated the provisions of the agreement, would the Serb side then be released from its obligation arising from the agreement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that context I believe that they would, and certainly within the framework of my own analysis, I've always conceded the fact that the 28th Infantry Division was never disarmed and that it was an armed entity and, therefore, was subject to attack by the Army of Republika Srpska. I mean, the division itself represents a legitimate military target. So I don't believe we're in disagreement on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just to try to make clear, nor is the Prosecution in disagreement, as for many years now that's been our position. Just to remind the general on that particular point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Prosecution has repeated this position quite often. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In that case let's turn to page 9 of the statement D193, which is General Smith's statement. Page 9 in Serbian, paragraph 4. Thank you. That's page 9, paragraph 2 in English. Thank you, Aleksandar. Thank you. We can see it. In the paragraph above, which we quoted a moment ago, Mladic referred to the need to demilitarise the zone and stated what boundaries they should be reduced to. And now paragraph 4 in Serbian and 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I am quoting Mladic's -- or, rather, Smith's words: "Mladic said that his concerns about Bosnian Army's intentions had led him to restrict the amount of food, medicine, and fuel for the enclaves and claimed that the United Nations was supplying the Bosnian Army. I replied that any attack on the UN safe areas would be condemned by the international community ..." This is my question: Is it the case that here Mr. Smith responded to Mladic's statement or in fact retorted by referring to the possibility of threat applied by the United Nations? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, not wanting to put words in General Smith's mouth, I mean, what General Smith was -- at least in his own statement was saying back to General Mladic was that any attack on the UN safe areas would be condemned by the international community and would risk a response by NATO air power against the Bosnian Serbs. Whether that qualified as an abstract laying out of the consequences or whether it's a retort with nothing behind it is something you would have to ask General Smith. I would say that when you look at what happened in June and July, certainly in Sarajevo and to a far lesser degree in Srebrenica, NATO air power was employed. So General Smith was at least accurately laying out that he had a capability to deal, or at least to inflict, those types of consequences if he believed the safe areas were violated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. As you can see, General Mladic cautioned about the Muslims violating the agreement, and Smith said that they would be bombed if they attack. Although, this is permitted for a party conferring upon an area the status of a demilitarised zone under Article 6 of Protocol 1. This is my question: Did, by acting this way, General Smith comply with the provisions of the Geneva Conventions or did he in fact side with the Muslims who were mounting attacks out of the demilitarised zone, an issue that we were discussing earlier today? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can't tell you whether or not General Smith was or was not in compliance with the conventions. What I can say is that the Bosnia Serb military leadership and political leadership at the time believed, particularly with respect to the enclaves, that UNPROFOR was biased towards the Bosnian Muslims in them and that this would be a reflection of that. That was a widely-held belief by many of the senior leadership of the VRS, that, either directly or indirectly, the United Nations forces were helping the Bosnian Muslim military forces in the enclaves and in and around the Sarajevo safe area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's see what the position of the political leadership of Republika Srpska was in respect of the enclaves and what Mr. Karadzic had to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 11, paragraph 4 in Serbian, which is page 11, paragraph 1 in English. Thank you, Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I am reading from the third line of the paragraph. "Karadzic said that the VRS would not be respecting the safe areas and claimed that they were unlawful under international law. He also claimed that the BH Army was attacking them on a regular basis out of Srebrenica and that the VRS was -- had sustained casualties." Is it not the case that here both the political and military leadership told General Smith that the areas were not demilitarised, that they were used for mounting attacks against the party which conferred upon them the status of demilitarised zones?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with the fact that both General -- I'm sorry, President Karadzic and General Mladic were both consistent in their message back to General Smith that their view was because of the fact that the zones were not demilitarised, that they believed that they had the ability to militarily attack into them. So both President Karadzic and General Mladic delivered a very consistent message to General Smith here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Did they also send a message that they would restrict the supplies to the enclaves, not only the message that they were under attack?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, as evidenced by the earlier paragraph that we read, General Mladic made it clear that he was going to restrict humanitarian supplies going in to the enclaves because it was his belief that those humanitarian supplies were being used for military purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look, while we still have time, at page 12 of this statement by Smith, paragraph 2, the last three sentences. It's page 11 in English, towards the bottom of the page. It says: "He made a series of unrealistic demands such as the lifting of sanctions in return for an extension of the cessation of hostilities agreement. I raised the issue of direct attacks on UNPROFOR and the denial of supplies to the UNPROFOR troops in the enclaves. Karadzic denied responsibility for attacks on UNPROFOR personnel, but accepted that there had been mistakes. He then made the point that he could not respect United Nations safe areas, claiming them to be illegal in international law. "On the issue of fuel, General Gvero said that fuel was to be denied to UN troops in the enclaves because he had evidence that in particular the UN troops in Srebrenica were supplying the Bosnian Army with fuel. Gvero also said that he had intelligence that UNPROFOR had adequate reserves of fuel." At these meetings also with the political leadership, was it announced to General Smith that supplies to the UNPROFOR in the enclaves must be limited because they were making them available to Bosnian Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, given the fact that this is General Smith's statement, he is certainly coming away with that message. So I take it from notes and his recollections of the meetings that he was very clear in the context of who was saying what and what the basis for those discussions were. In this particular case, he makes it clear that President Karadzic is citing General Gvero and information that he has about fuel being diverting to the Bosnian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now look at page 13, if you please, paragraph 3 in Serbian. And that's page 12 in English, the last paragraph. Thank you, Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I quote the beginning of that paragraph: "On the 9th of May, I had a further private meeting with Dr. Karadzic. The discussions covered the recent Bosnian Serb army attacks on Sarajevo and the Bosnian Serb sanctions on the UN contingents in the eastern enclaves." And then he says: "I explained why I had recommended NATO air-strikes," et cetera. In this paragraph 2, isn't it the case that president of Republika Srpska announces and informs General Smith that he had imposed sanctions on the UN troops in the enclaves -- in the eastern enclaves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe it's just a language issue. I take this that -- not necessarily Dr. Karadzic making a declaration that he has made formal sanctions against the UN contingents, but General Smith's discussion which is, you know, his understanding of basically why that he considers the -- that there are to be Bosnian Serb sanctions on the UN contingent. Now, I guess taking this in line with the other exhibits that we've discussed during the Prosecution case where as a matter of policy the Main Staff was doing these types of things, I guess at the pinnacle of that you're correct in saying that President Karadzic ultimately made this decision. But, I mean, when I read this paragraph in isolation, that meaning doesn't come out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I am forced to quote again his exact words. He says: "The discussions covered the recent BSA attacks in Sarajevo and the Bosnian Serb sanctions on the UN contingents in the eastern enclaves." He doesn't say the army imposed sanctions. He says Bosnian Serbs. And he discussed these two problems on the 9th May with President Karadzic, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, the issues came up on the 9th of May. The exact phrase, again, from -- this isn't General Smith quoting President Karadzic. This is General Smith's statement where he says: "The discussions covered the recent attacks on Sarajevo and the Bosnian Serb sanctions on the UN contingents." Now, I don't know whether that's an exact quote from President Karadzic or not. I did not follow General Smith's testimony.
